A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same softmax-dispersion theory and adaptive-temperature approach. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated or renumbered in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original maximum-retrieval experiments, Gemma attention measurements, and comparative CLRS-Text fine-tuning results in Table 1 and Figures 2–7.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experimental studies and adds empirical logit-spread measurements, numerical validation of the spectral-norm bound, and reported streaming-implementation checks.

M1.justification: Appendix G introduces a streaming entropy-computation procedure intended to support linear-memory adaptive attention. The core entropy-conditioned polynomial rule, retrieval architecture, and use of adaptive temperature during Gemma fine-tuning remain unchanged. Appendix F primarily explains how the existing temperature rule was derived.

E1.justification: Maximum retrieval and the same thirty CLRS-Text tasks remain. Section 2 adds attention diagnostics using an approximately 4,000-token source-code sample, extending the represented inputs beyond the earlier numerical and algorithmic examples without introducing a new benchmark.

E2.justification: The retrieval comparison remains ordinary softmax versus adaptive temperature, and CLRS-Text still compares Gemma 2B fine-tuned with and without adaptation. Newly discussed methods such as AERO, selective attention, and Differential Transformer are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New evaluations measure pretrained Gemma 2B/7B logit spreads, track the spectral bound during retrieval-model training, and check streaming computation up to 131,072 tokens. The stated original retrieval training settings and CLRS-Text 2,048-token output limit remain unchanged. Newly disclosed fitting details do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds focused diagnostics of practical logit spreads and a training-trajectory comparison between observed spread and Proposition 3.1's bound (Appendix D, Figure 9). Appendix G also reports numerical agreement checks for streaming computation. Existing attention visualizations and temperature-sensitivity analysis are retained.

E5.justification: The expanded Figure 3 caption identifies the existing shaded summary as the mean and standard deviation across attention heads, information unspecified in v1. Table 1 retains ten-seed averaging and paired t-tests. Changed CLRS-Text uncertainty bands do not establish a changed statistical procedure or increased run count.

E6.justification: Although Table 1 is identical, adaptive-temperature accuracy curves and uncertainty bands change across many CLRS-Text tasks, including Dijkstra and MST Prim (v1 Figure 7; v3 Figure 8). v3 also adds Gemma logit-spread values, spectral-bound training trajectories, and reported streaming agreement and scalability results. The reason for the revised CLRS-Text curves is not specified.

T1.justification: New Appendix B develops a finite-precision misclassification corollary and extensions; Appendix C adds reasoning about dispersion across depth, residual connections, and causal attention; Appendix G derives streaming recurrences. The original proposition proofs survive as Appendices D and E. These additions substantially extend the mathematical arguments, although some new reasoning has correctness issues.

C1.justification: The central dispersion and adaptive-mitigation contributions remain. v3 explicitly frames the problem as size generalisation and qualifies the conclusion through architectural choices such as tokenisation and global attention. Its introduction also makes the connection from dispersion to prediction failures explicit through the new corollaries.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands explanations of practical logit bounds, dispersion across layers, and the roles of residual and causal attention. It cautiously attributes underperformance on Heapsort, MST Kruskal, and Bubble Sort to contexts exceeding the polynomial-fitting regime, and distinguishes how additional attention alternatives might evade dispersion.

D1.justification: Appendix F supplies the temperature-fitting grid from 0 to 10 in increments of 0.1 and a fuller fitting recipe. v3 corrects the printed polynomial's coefficient order and provides more precise coefficients in code. Appendix G adds implementation recurrences, an NVIDIA A100 hardware disclosure, and the reported 131,072-token capacity.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against prior temperature-adaptation approaches, distinguishing classification-layer, length-dependent, learnable-temperature, and entropy-based approaches. It adds discussion of AERO, Entropix, FlashAttention, length/size generalisation, and selective, differential, sparse, and stick-breaking attention while retaining the original mechanistic-interpretability background.

P1.justification: Beyond the revised title, v3 extensively expands the introductory explanation with a key-result overview and an attention/Transformer primer. It adds a step-by-step account of temperature fitting, clarifies experimental descriptions and terminology, reorganizes the appendices, and adds an impact statement.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main-text layout and extensively relocates and resizes displays. The entropy heatmap becomes four panels, the adaptive-temperature code becomes Figure 4, captions gain explanatory detail, and Figure 9 adds the spectral-bound plot. Several original figures are retained with new numbering and placement.

improvement.justification: v3 improves exposition, research positioning, and reproducibility, notably by correcting the polynomial caption and documenting fitting. However, new Appendix G computes the negative of the Shannon entropy defined in Equation 16: its final expression gives -log n for uniform attention. Appendix C also infers exact uniform averaging from small coefficients without establishing that implication. These problems undermine important new implementation and theoretical support, making the net quality benefit uncertain despite the useful additions.
